page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E6.Flex.4-16 is a virtual machine instance based on the AMD EPYC 9J45 processor utilizing the x86_64 architecture. The instance is configured with 4 dedicated physical cores running at a base clock speed of 2.7 GHz, delivering 8 vCPUs across simultaneous multithreading with 2 threads per core. System memory totals 16.0 GB of RAM, allocating 2.0 GB of memory per core.

The instance includes 1 complimentary public IPv4 address and does not include integrated local disk storage. Workloads deployed on this shape depend entirely on remote block volumes or network-attached storage for persistent state, introducing network I/O considerations for disk-heavy tasks. From an architectural perspective, the 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio prioritizes processing capacity relative to footprint size, offering resource allocation efficiency for tasks where large memory tables are unnecessary.

Given the compute-biased memory configuration and dedicated AMD EPYC core allocation, VM.Standard.E6.Flex.4-16 is configured for CPU-centric tasks. Representative deployment scenarios include web serving, continuous integration and build pipelines, batch processing jobs, and horizontally scaled application tiers that do not demand extensive in-memory caching.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E6.Flex.4-16 is an x86_64 virtual machine instance powered by an AMD EPYC 9J45 processor operating at 2.7 GHz. The hardware profile provides 4 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs via multithreading, provisioned alongside 16.0 GB of RAM, establishing a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio with 2.0 GB per core. The instance provides 1 complimentary public IPv4 address and contains no local storage, requiring external network block storage for persistent data requirements. With dedicated core assignment and no hardware GPU accelerators, the compute density favors computational throughput over broad memory caching. VM.Standard.E6.Flex.4-16 aligns with workloads such as web serving, continuous integration runners, batch processing, and microservices where compute execution takes precedence over substantial memory retention.
